presentation.title: OpenGame 投资人汇报（中文优化版）

content.p: Simulate, predict, and steer real-world outcomes —
before they happen in the real world.

OpenGame is a world simulation and forecasting engine. We build a living digital twin of a community, run its future forward thousands of times, and inject decisions and rumors to see what happens next. The game is just the visible skin; the core product is the ability to predict and steer real-world outcomes before they happen. Over the next few minutes I will cover the problem, our technology, the business model, and why we are positioned to win.
Fixed dashboards and single-point forecasts cannot show how crowds, rumors, and reactions compound into outcomes nobody predicted.

strong.span: Real-world trials are slow and irreversible.

content.p: Testing a policy, deployment, or message in the real world takes weeks and costs money — and cannot be undone once people are harmed.
Sentiment and disinformation spread in hours; by the time a report is written, the crowd has already made up its mind.

Today, anyone responsible for a high-stakes decision faces three structural problems. First, static models miss emergence — they cannot capture how crowds, rumors, and reactions compound. Second, testing in the real world is slow, expensive, and irreversible. Third, disinformation spreads faster than any analyst can write a report. The gap between how fast the world moves and how fast we can understand it is the problem we solve.

OpenGame builds a living, checkable, playable digital twin of a community from a single prompt. We run its future thousands of times, inject decisions and rumors, and read out what happens — before reality does.

Our answer is a living digital twin. Instead of reasoning about the world from a static model, you build a checkable, playable community that runs on its own, and you run its future forward. You inject the decision you are considering, or a rumor, and watch how it spreads. The loop is simple: simulate, intervene, forecast. That loop is the core of the product, and it is what the next slide shows in detail.
We don't predict once — we run a closed loop, and every run sharpens the forecast.

This is the heart of the product. We do not produce a single forecast and walk away. We run a closed loop: the living world simulates forward, we intervene with a decision or a rumor, we observe how the crowd reacts, we turn that into a probability forecast, and the decision-maker acts. Acting changes the world, which feeds the next simulation. Because every run is compared against what actually happened, the engine gets more calibrated over time.
One engine, four ways to read the world before it moves.

The same engine produces four distinct outputs. First, opinion and sentiment: we track grievance, legitimacy and mood for every resident. Second, scenario simulation: we replay a decision or a rumor inside a living world that can be checked. Third, probabilistic forecasting: we return P10 to P90 outcomes calibrated against historical cases. Fourth, decision support: we compare options, test sensitivity, and let the decision-maker act. These are not four separate products; they are four reads of one simulated world.
Symbolic truth at the core, neural dynamics as advisor, rendering as a skin.
Phaser / Three / LingBot / Marble — a playable skin; if the video breaks, the 2D game still runs
Small networks imagine action consequences — advise only, never rewrite L1
Residents with memory, plans, needs, and opinion & rumor dynamics
World Spec (single source of truth) · deterministic simulator · WorldOp version lineage

Pure neural world models hallucinate and cannot be checked; pure symbolic engines are rigid. We combine them. At the bottom is L1, symbolic truth: a typed World Spec, a deterministic simulator, and versioned WorldOps that can be rolled back. Above it sits the living society of residents. L2 is a small neural layer that imagines consequences and can only advise, never overwrite L1. L3 is the render layer, a playable skin. If the video breaks, the 2D game still runs because L1 keeps the world consistent. This is why our worlds are both generative and checkable.
Every world is a typed, versioned specification — reproducible and auditable.
Schema-validated; one single source of truth
Same inputs, same outcomes — fully reproducible
Typed mutations with a revision lineage; roll back any step

Video world models give you pixels you cannot verify. Our world is a typed specification, validated by schema, with one source of truth. The simulator is deterministic: the same inputs always produce the same world, so a result can be reproduced. Every change is a typed WorldOp that records its parent, forming a revision lineage. You can inspect why a resident did something and roll back to any earlier state. A world that can be checked and replayed is trustworthy in a way that a generated video never is. That is the first layer of the moat.
We compile intent into a contract, then verify the world honors it.
retry until every promise is honored

Generative systems either hallucinate or quietly collapse into the same default town. We prevent both. A natural-language prompt is first compiled into a typed intent, then into a promise contract: the genre, the place, the jobs, and the population the author commits to. The world is generated against that contract, and a gate checks every promise before release. If a promise is missing, the system regenerates instead of shipping a template. What the author promises is what the world demonstrably contains. That makes output both creative and guaranteed.
Residents are not scripted NPCs — they remember, plan, need, form opinions, and wonder.
Inside every heartbeat: an inner world model

Each resident is a living agent: they hold memory, keep a daily plan, have four needs that can interrupt that plan, and run opinion dynamics that become grievance, legitimacy, and rumors. The key addition is an inner world model running inside every heartbeat. A resident predicts where the crowd will be next, then compares that with what actually happens. The gap is surprise, which raises curiosity and drives the resident to walk over and look. Because attention is earned by surprise rather than scripted, behavior is genuinely emergent; a gate guards the emergence and a template is the fallback. This is a society that lives on its own.
An ensemble of simulated futures, turned into calibrated probability bands.
Calibrated on historical cases: Brier score,

We do not output a single guess. The engine runs a Monte Carlo ensemble of futures, seeded from two presets: a contested decision and an exercise near a residential area. Each run is a complete simulation, and the ensemble becomes a probability distribution: P10, P50, and P90 bands for turnout, casualties, hotspots, and the escalation timeline, together with the causal chain, alternatives, and a sensitivity analysis. Crucially, those probabilities are calibrated against a library of historical cases, using a Brier score, case distance, and interval coverage. That means the number we call 80 percent actually happens about 80 percent of the time. This is a forecast you can trust and audit, not a confident hallucination.
Decision support: run the what-ifs first
Compare interventions, see their outcomes, and know which assumptions drive them.
Sensitivity: which assumptions move the result most — crowd size, rumor speed, force posture.

Before acting in the real world, a decision-maker can run every option: hold, de-escalate, or deter. Each intervention is simulated as a full ensemble, so the decision-maker sees not just a predicted outcome but the probability band around it, the casualties and turnout implied, and the risk of a sudden spike. In this illustrative comparison, opening dialogue lowers the median escalation while holding leaves it high; deterrence can work but carries a tail risk. A sensitivity analysis then shows which assumptions, such as crowd size or rumor speed, move the result most. The system does not make the decision, but it makes the trade-offs visible and comparable before anyone commits.
The same living world is both a forecasting object and a game you can play.
If the video layer fails, the 2D world keeps running and stays playable.

There is one world, but it presents two surfaces. To an observer or a forecaster it is an object to watch, simulate, and place predictions on. To a player, that same world is a game to enter and alter. Both sit on the identical checkable, living core, so a player's action and a forecaster's prediction are about the same evolving reality. This is why the product is not a game and not a forecasting tool: it is a world that supports both. The architecture also degrades gracefully: if the 3D or video layer fails, the 2D game stays playable, and the world itself keeps running. One world, two ways in, no single point of failure.
Attention is free; we monetize the prediction and the drama, not the visit.
Most of the rake goes to the author
The product is the drama card
First card half price to pull players in
Authors pay to activate their world (light today / this week). Visitors are never charged per visit.

The business model has two tracks over the same world. On the world track, watching is free and the product is the prediction: users place bets, and the platform takes a 15 percent rake, most of which goes to the author. On the game track, playing is free and the product is drama cards: small, reversible in-world enhancements, with 70 percent to the author and a half-price first card to pull new players in. On the cost side, authors pay to activate their world, lighting it for today or this week, while the platform never charges a visitor per visit. This aligns everyone: authors earn from both tracks, visitors pay only for the moments they choose, and the platform is paid for outcomes rather than access.
One world, one market — settled by the world's own evidence, never by the author.
Settled by real dialogue and living evidence
The author cannot change the verdict
The author cannot bet on their own market
15% rake; 70% of it to the author
Winners split the rest; 8x cap per bet
One-sided, silent, stopped, or tied: full refund

Each world runs one market, seeded automatically. The lock point is set at 12, 24, or 48 hours. The market opens, closes four hours later, and then spends four hours gathering evidence. The verdict comes from the town's real dialogue and living evidence, not from the author, who cannot change the result and cannot bet on their own market. A market forms only when both sides have stakes. The platform takes 15 percent, 70 percent of that goes to the author, and winners split the rest, with an 8x cap per bet. If the market is one-sided, silent, the clock stops, or the result is tied, every stake is refunded. The rules are designed to be fair and self-policing, which is what makes strangers willing to bet.
Why users come back on day two
The world keeps running while you are away, and it leaves open reasons to return.
While you are away, residents keep living
come back to see it settle
come back to find what is new
Same-day returning players earn a multiplier.

Most generated content is consumed once and never revisited. A living world is different because it does not pause when the user leaves. Residents keep living, opinions keep moving, and the clock on any open prediction keeps running. That gives three concrete reasons to return: a prediction that is still open and waiting to settle, a world that has visibly changed overnight, and a personal story that is still in motion. We reinforce the habit on the game track with a multiplier for same-day returning players. Retention here is not a notification strategy; it is a structural consequence of a world that genuinely continues. The product has a tomorrow, which is the first thing a recurring-revenue business needs.
Others build one layer. We combine a playable, checkable, living world with a market on it.

This table shows why we do not see a direct competitor. Chat-to-code tools generate code, but they have no checkable world, no continuous society, and no market. Video world models produce impressive clips, but they are not truly playable or auditable. The NPC-town research pioneered living agents, but those demos are not playable, not checkable, and not monetized. OpenGame is the only system that combines all five: a playable surface, a checkable world, continuous living evolution, opinion and rumor dynamics, and a prediction market on top. The moat is not any single feature; it is the combination, because each layer makes the others more valuable. A competitor would have to build all five at once, and they are already integrated and running.
The same engine generates entirely different genres, each end-to-end and playable.
Genre, art, layout, and core loop are generated from one sentence — not stitched from templates.
Each demo ships as a working game with a documented mechanic spec and a downloadable build.

This is the system working today. From one sentence each, the engine produced four different genres: a platformer, two top-down games, and a tower defense. The art, the layout, the camera, and the core gameplay loop are all generated, not assembled from a fixed template. Each one is a genuinely playable game, with a documented mechanic spec and a downloadable build. The point for investors is twofold: the generation is real and genre-agnostic, and the same engine that produces these worlds is the engine that runs our forecasts. The playable surface proves the world underneath is coherent. We are not showing a concept; we are showing working worlds.
Roadmap: from worlds to a market
The hard technical layer is built; the next phases turn it into a marketplace and an ecosystem.

The roadmap is sequenced so the hardest science comes first and the marketplace follows. Today, world generation and the forecasting core are working. Next, we expand the historical case library that calibrates our probabilities and launch the prediction market. Then we open the author ecosystem and turn on both revenue tracks, so authors create the worlds we monetize. In year two, we extend the engine from the current community and civic scenarios into broader domains such as cities, crises, and public events. Each phase compounds the last: more worlds improve calibration, better calibration drives betting, and betting funds more authors. We are raising now to move from the technical foundation, which is proven, to the marketplace and the supply side.
We would rather show you the edges of the system than overclaim it.
We show P10–P90 bands and calibrate them; true black swans stay open.
Output depends on the quality of the world spec
Typed specs and deterministic simulation keep inputs honest.
Calibration needs a large historical case library
We expand it continuously and disclose the nearest-case distance.
Generation can still fail on edge cases
Gates plus a template fallback; a human reviews before release.
This is decision support. We make the trade-offs visible; the human still decides.

We want to be candid about what the system is and is not. It outputs probabilities, not certainties, and a genuinely unprecedented event cannot be forecast; we show the bands and keep the tails open. The quality of a prediction depends on the quality of the world spec, which is why specs are typed and the simulator is deterministic. Calibration is only as good as the case library, and we are growing it while disclosing how close the nearest case is. On edge cases, generation can still fail, so gates and a template fallback protect the output and a human reviews. The system is a decision aid that makes trade-offs visible, not a replacement for judgment. We believe this honesty is itself a reason to trust the numbers.
A playable, checkable, living world — with a forecasting market on top.
We would love to walk you through a live world and discuss the round.

To close, the idea is simple. Most systems react to the world after it moves. We run the world forward first, inside a living, checkable simulation, and let people place predictions on what comes next. The game is the skin; the moat is the combination of a checkable world, promise-constrained generation, and a living society, and the business is a two-track model with a self-policing prediction market. We would be glad to walk you through a live world and answer questions. Thank you.
